CHAPTER 29 - SOME COMMON HUMAN DISEASES

Introduction

Good health is more than the mere absence of illness. The World Health Organisation defines HEALTH as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. A DISEASE, on the other hand, is any disturbance in the normal structure or functioning of the body (or a part of it) that produces recognisable signs and symptoms. This chapter surveys the common diseases that affect human beings, the organisms and conditions that cause them, how they spread, how the body defends itself, and how diseases can be prevented and controlled through immunisation and hygiene.

29.1 HEALTH AND DISEASE

The word disease literally means dis-ease, a lack of ease or comfort. When the body works normally we say a person is healthy; when its working is upset by an internal disorder or an outside agent, we say the person is diseased. SYMPTOMS are the changes a patient feels and reports (pain, fever, weakness), while SIGNS are the changes a doctor can observe or measure (raised temperature, swelling, abnormal blood counts). Health depends on balanced nutrition, clean water, sanitation, exercise, rest, and a disease-free environment. Poverty, malnutrition, pollution and lack of hygiene make people more vulnerable to disease.

29.2 CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES

Diseases may be classified in several ways. A basic division is into CONGENITAL and ACQUIRED diseases.

CONGENITAL diseases are present from birth. They arise from genetic defects (mutations, chromosomal abnormalities) or from problems during development in the womb. Examples include colour blindness, haemophilia, sickle-cell anaemia, Down's syndrome and cleft palate. They are generally permanent and often inherited.

ACQUIRED diseases develop after birth during a person's lifetime. They are further divided into COMMUNICABLE (infectious) and NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases.

COMMUNICABLE or INFECTIOUS diseases are caused by pathogens (disease-causing organisms) and can spread from an infected person to a healthy person. Examples include tuberculosis, cholera, influenza, malaria and AIDS.

NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases do NOT spread from person to person. They arise from lifestyle, ageing, deficiency, degeneration, or malfunction of body organs. Examples include cancer, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and arthritis.

29.3 INFECTIOUS DISEASES AND THEIR PATHOGENS

An infectious disease is caused by a PATHOGEN - a bacterium, virus, protozoan, fungus or worm - that enters the body, multiplies, and damages tissues. The pathogens are grouped by the kind of organism that causes them.

BACTERIAL DISEASES

Bacteria are microscopic single-celled organisms. Some cause disease by multiplying in tissues and releasing poisonous substances called TOXINS. Important bacterial diseases are:

- TUBERCULOSIS (TB): caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It mainly affects the lungs but can attack other organs. It spreads through droplets released when a patient coughs or sneezes. Symptoms include persistent cough (often with blood), fever, night sweats and weight loss. It is prevented by the BCG vaccine and treated with a long course of antibiotics under the DOTS programme.

- CHOLERA: caused by Vibrio cholerae. It spreads through contaminated water and food. It causes severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting, leading to rapid dehydration. Prevention lies in clean water, sanitation and oral rehydration therapy for treatment.

- TYPHOID: caused by Salmonella typhi, spread through contaminated food and water. Symptoms include sustained high fever, headache, weakness and abdominal pain. The Widal test helps diagnosis; prevention is by hygiene and vaccination.

- TETANUS (lockjaw): caused by Clostridium tetani, whose spores enter the body through deep wounds. Its toxin causes painful muscle spasms and stiffness, especially of the jaw. It is prevented by the DPT vaccine and tetanus toxoid injections.

- PNEUMONIA: an infection of the lungs often caused by the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae. It causes fever, chills, cough and difficulty in breathing. It spreads by droplets and is treated with antibiotics.

- DIPHTHERIA: caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, affecting the throat. It produces a greyish membrane in the throat, fever and difficulty in breathing. It spreads by droplets and is prevented by the DPT vaccine.

VIRAL DISEASES

Viruses are extremely small infectious agents that can multiply only inside living cells. Antibiotics do NOT work against viruses; prevention through vaccines is the key. Important viral diseases are:

- COMMON COLD: caused by rhinoviruses. It brings sneezing, running nose, sore throat and mild fever. It spreads by droplets and contact and usually clears on its own.

- INFLUENZA (flu): caused by the influenza virus. It causes fever, body ache, cough and fatigue, and spreads by droplets. Vaccines are available and change each year as the virus mutates.

- MEASLES: caused by the measles virus. It brings fever and a characteristic skin rash and spreads by droplets. It is prevented by the MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine.

- POLIOMYELITIS (polio): caused by the poliovirus, spread through contaminated water and food. It can damage nerves and cause paralysis, especially in children. It is prevented by the oral polio vaccine (OPV); the Pulse Polio programme has nearly eradicated it in India.

- HEPATITIS: inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis viruses (types A, B, C, etc.). Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water; hepatitis B and C spread through blood, body fluids and unsafe injections. Symptoms include jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes), fever and fatigue. Vaccines exist for hepatitis A and B.

- RABIES: caused by the rabies virus, transmitted by the bite of an infected dog or other animal. It affects the nervous system and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. Anti-rabies vaccination immediately after a bite prevents the disease.

- DENGUE: caused by the dengue virus, transmitted by the bite of the Aedes mosquito, which breeds in clean stagnant water. It causes high fever, severe joint and muscle pain, headache and, in severe cases, bleeding. Prevention lies in controlling mosquito breeding.

- AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome): caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), which attacks and destroys the helper T-lymphocytes of the immune system, so the body loses its ability to fight infections. HIV spreads through unprotected sexual contact, transfusion of infected blood, sharing of infected needles, and from an infected mother to her child. It does NOT spread by touch, sharing food, mosquito bites or casual contact. There is no complete cure, but anti-retroviral therapy prolongs life; prevention through awareness and safe practices is essential.

- COVID-19: caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus. It spreads mainly through respiratory droplets and close contact. Symptoms include fever, dry cough, tiredness and loss of taste or smell; severe cases cause breathing difficulty. Prevention includes masks, hand washing, physical distancing and vaccination.

PROTOZOAN DISEASES

Protozoa are single-celled animal-like organisms. Important protozoan diseases are:

- MALARIA: caused by the protozoan Plasmodium (species such as P. vivax and P. falciparum) and transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. The parasite has a two-host life cycle: it multiplies asexually in the human liver and red blood cells, and reproduces sexually in the mosquito. When an infected female Anopheles bites a person, it injects sporozoites; these reach the liver, multiply, then enter red blood cells and destroy them, releasing toxins that cause the typical cycles of chill, high fever and sweating. When another mosquito bites the patient it takes up the parasite, completing the cycle. Prevention lies in destroying mosquito breeding places, using nets and repellents, and treatment with antimalarial drugs.

- AMOEBIASIS (amoebic dysentery): caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, which lives in the large intestine. It spreads through food and water contaminated with faeces (often by houseflies). It causes abdominal pain and stools with mucus and blood.

- KALA-AZAR (visceral leishmaniasis): caused by the protozoan Leishmania and transmitted by the bite of the sandfly. It causes prolonged fever, weakness, weight loss and enlargement of the spleen and liver.

FUNGAL DISEASES

Fungi are simple plant-like organisms that lack chlorophyll. RINGWORM is a common fungal disease of the skin caused by fungi such as Microsporum and Trichophyton. It produces dry, scaly, ring-shaped patches on the skin, scalp or nails that itch. It spreads by contact with infected persons, animals or objects (combs, towels) and is favoured by heat and moisture. Athlete's foot is a related fungal infection.

HELMINTHIC (WORM) DISEASES

Helminths are parasitic worms. Important worm diseases are:

- ASCARIASIS: caused by the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, which lives in the intestine. Its eggs spread through contaminated food and water. It causes abdominal pain, indigestion and blockage.

- FILARIASIS (elephantiasis): caused by the thread-like filarial worm Wuchereria, transmitted by the Culex mosquito. The worms block the lymph vessels, causing gross swelling of the legs and other parts.

- TAENIASIS: caused by the tapeworm Taenia, whose larvae enter through undercooked pork or beef. The worm lives in the intestine and robs the host of nutrients.

29.4 MODES OF TRANSMISSION

Infectious diseases spread from a source to a healthy host in several ways: (1) AIR (droplets from coughing and sneezing) - tuberculosis, common cold, influenza, measles, COVID-19; (2) WATER and FOOD contaminated with pathogens - cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, polio, amoebiasis; (3) VECTORS (insects that carry pathogens) - malaria (Anopheles mosquito), dengue (Aedes mosquito), filariasis (Culex mosquito), kala-azar (sandfly); (4) CONTACT, direct or through objects - ringworm, and through sexual contact or blood - AIDS, hepatitis B; (5) ANIMAL BITES - rabies. Knowing the mode of spread is the key to breaking the chain and preventing the disease.

29.5 IMMUNITY

IMMUNITY is the ability of the body to resist and fight off pathogens. It is of two broad kinds.

INNATE (natural or non-specific) immunity is present from birth and acts against any invader. Its defences include the skin and mucous membranes (physical barriers), acids and enzymes in secretions (chemical barriers), and phagocytic white blood cells that engulf germs, together with inflammation and fever.

ACQUIRED (adaptive or specific) immunity develops during life after exposure to a particular pathogen. It is specific and has memory - the body responds faster on a second exposure. Acquired immunity is of two types:

- ACTIVE immunity is produced by the body's own cells when it meets an antigen, either through natural infection or through vaccination. It develops slowly but lasts long because memory cells are formed.

- PASSIVE immunity is borrowed - ready-made antibodies are given to the body from outside. Examples are antibodies passed from mother to baby through the placenta and breast milk, and injections of antiserum (such as anti-tetanus serum). It acts immediately but is short-lived.

ANTIGENS AND ANTIBODIES: An ANTIGEN is any foreign substance (usually a protein on a pathogen) that triggers an immune response. In reply the body's lymphocytes produce ANTIBODIES - special proteins that bind to the antigen and neutralise or destroy the pathogen. THE IMMUNE RESPONSE (in brief): when a pathogen enters, phagocytes engulf some of it and display its antigens; helper T-lymphocytes recognise these and activate B-lymphocytes, which multiply and secrete antibodies, while other cells kill infected cells. Some cells become MEMORY cells that remember the antigen for years, giving long-lasting protection.

29.6 VACCINATION AND IMMUNISATION

VACCINATION (immunisation) is the deliberate introduction of a vaccine - a preparation of weakened, killed or fragments of a pathogen (or its toxoid) - into the body to stimulate active immunity WITHOUT causing the disease. The vaccine makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells, so that if the real pathogen attacks later, the body destroys it quickly.

Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine, against smallpox, and worldwide vaccination has since ERADICATED smallpox. India's Universal Immunisation Programme protects children against tuberculosis (BCG), diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and tetanus (DPT), polio (OPV), measles, hepatitis B and other diseases. The Pulse Polio programme has made India polio-free. Vaccination protects not only the individual but, when enough people are immune, the whole community (herd immunity).

29.7 NON-COMMUNICABLE AND LIFESTYLE DISEASES

These diseases do not spread from person to person. Many are linked to modern lifestyle - poor diet, lack of exercise, obesity, stress, smoking and alcohol.

- CANCER is uncontrolled, abnormal multiplication of body cells that lose the normal checks on division. The mass of such cells is a tumour; a malignant (cancerous) tumour can invade nearby tissues and spread to distant organs (metastasis). Cancers are named by their site, such as lung cancer, breast cancer, blood cancer (leukaemia) and skin cancer. Causes include tobacco and alcohol, radiation, certain chemicals (carcinogens), some viruses and heredity. Early detection and treatment by surgery, radiation or chemotherapy improve the chance of cure.

- DIABETES MELLITUS results when the pancreas fails to produce enough of the hormone INSULIN, or the body cannot use it, so blood sugar rises. Symptoms include frequent urination, excessive thirst and hunger, and weakness. It is controlled by diet, exercise, medicines and, when needed, insulin.

- CARDIOVASCULAR (HEART) DISEASE includes conditions in which the heart and blood vessels are damaged, such as narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty deposits, which can cause a heart attack. Risk factors are a fatty diet, obesity, smoking, lack of exercise and high blood pressure.

- HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure) is persistently raised blood pressure. It usually has no obvious symptoms but strains the heart, blood vessels, kidneys and brain and can lead to heart attack and stroke. It is controlled by a low-salt diet, exercise, weight control and medicines.

29.8 DRUG AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

A DRUG is a chemical that alters the working of the body. Some drugs are valuable medicines, but many are misused. DRUG ABUSE is the use of a drug for a purpose other than medical, in a way that harms the body and mind. Commonly abused substances include opioids (opium, heroin), cannabinoids (ganja, charas), cocaine, and depressants and stimulants, as well as tobacco and alcohol.

ADDICTION (dependence) is a state in which a person cannot do without the drug; stopping it produces unpleasant WITHDRAWAL symptoms. Repeated use also builds TOLERANCE, so larger doses are needed. Drug and alcohol abuse damages the liver, brain, heart and nervous system, impairs judgement, and destroys studies, work, family and social life. ALCOHOL abuse damages the liver (cirrhosis), and drunk driving causes accidents. Tobacco (smoking and chewing) causes cancer of the lung and mouth, and heart and lung disease. Prevention lies in awareness, saying no to peer pressure, seeking help from counsellors and de-addiction centres, and support from family and friends.

29.9 PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF DISEASES

Diseases are prevented and controlled by breaking the chain of infection and by strengthening the body. Key measures are:

- PERSONAL HYGIENE: washing hands before eating and after using the toilet, bathing, keeping nails clean, brushing teeth, and using clean clothes.

- COMMUNITY HYGIENE: a safe supply of drinking water, proper disposal of sewage and garbage, control of insects and rodents, clean surroundings, and safe food handling.

- BALANCED NUTRITION AND HEALTHY LIVING: nourishing food, exercise, rest and avoidance of tobacco, alcohol and drugs raise the body's resistance.

- VACCINATION of children and adults as per the immunisation schedule.

- ISOLATION of infected patients, sterilisation of instruments, safe blood transfusion and use of insect nets to check vector-borne diseases.

SUMMARY

- Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease; a disease is a disturbance of normal body function shown by signs and symptoms.
- Diseases are congenital (present from birth, often genetic) or acquired; acquired diseases are communicable (infectious) or non-communicable.
- Bacterial diseases include tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, pneumonia and diphtheria; viral diseases include the common cold, influenza, measles, polio, hepatitis, rabies, dengue, AIDS and COVID-19.
- Protozoan diseases include malaria (Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles), amoebiasis and kala-azar; ringworm is a fungal disease; ascariasis, filariasis and taeniasis are worm (helminthic) diseases.
- Diseases spread through air, water and food, vectors (insects), contact and animal bites; knowing the mode of spread guides prevention.
- Immunity is innate (present from birth, non-specific) or acquired (specific, with memory); acquired immunity is active (body-made, long-lasting) or passive (ready-made antibodies, short-lived). Antigens trigger antibodies made by lymphocytes.
- Vaccination introduces weakened or killed pathogens to build active immunity; it has eradicated smallpox and, through programmes like Pulse Polio, controls many childhood diseases.
- Non-communicable diseases include cancer (uncontrolled cell growth), diabetes (insulin failure), cardiovascular disease and hypertension, mostly linked to lifestyle.
- Drug and alcohol abuse leads to addiction, tolerance and withdrawal and damages body and life; prevention needs awareness and support.
- Diseases are controlled by personal and community hygiene, balanced nutrition, vaccination, isolation and vector control.

chapter_summary.title: Some Common Human Diseases - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary covers human health and disease. It classifies diseases; surveys bacterial, viral, protozoan, fungal and worm infections and how they spread; explains immunity and vaccination; describes lifestyle diseases and drug abuse; and outlines prevention through hygiene.

sections.heading: Health, disease and their classification
bullets: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.
Symptoms are felt and reported by the patient; signs are observed or measured by the doctor.
Congenital diseases are present from birth and often genetic; acquired diseases develop later in life.
Acquired diseases are communicable (infectious, spread by pathogens) or non-communicable (do not spread).

sections.heading: Bacterial and viral diseases
bullets: Bacterial diseases: tuberculosis (Mycobacterium), cholera (Vibrio), typhoid (Salmonella), tetanus, pneumonia, diphtheria.
Viral diseases: common cold, influenza, measles, polio, hepatitis, rabies, dengue, AIDS and COVID-19.
Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work against viruses, so viral diseases are prevented mainly by vaccines.
AIDS is caused by HIV, which destroys helper T-cells; it spreads by blood, sexual contact and mother to child, not by casual touch.

sections.heading: Protozoan, fungal and helminthic diseases
bullets: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito; it multiplies in the liver and red blood cells.
Amoebiasis (Entamoeba) and kala-azar (Leishmania, spread by sandfly) are other protozoan diseases.
Ringworm is a fungal skin disease spreading by contact and favoured by heat and moisture.
Worm diseases include ascariasis (roundworm), filariasis (Wuchereria, Culex mosquito) and taeniasis (tapeworm).

sections.heading: Immunity and vaccination
bullets: Innate immunity is present from birth and non-specific; acquired immunity is specific and has memory.
Active immunity is made by the body and long-lasting; passive immunity is ready-made antibodies and short-lived.
Antigens trigger lymphocytes to make antibodies; memory cells give lasting protection.
Vaccination introduces weakened or killed pathogens to build active immunity; it eradicated smallpox and controls polio.

sections.heading: Lifestyle diseases, drug abuse and prevention
bullets: Cancer is uncontrolled cell growth; diabetes results from insulin failure; hypertension is high blood pressure.
Drug and alcohol abuse cause addiction, tolerance and withdrawal and damage body and life.
Diseases spread by air, water, food, vectors, contact and bites, so breaking the chain prevents them.
Prevention relies on personal and community hygiene, nutrition, vaccination, isolation and vector control.

key_takeaways: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being; diseases are congenital or acquired, and acquired diseases are communicable or non-communicable.

Bacterial diseases (TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, pneumonia, diphtheria) are treated with antibiotics; viral diseases (cold, flu, measles, polio, hepatitis, rabies, dengue, AIDS, COVID-19) are prevented mainly by vaccines.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito; other pathogens include protozoa, fungi (ringworm) and worms (ascariasis, filariasis, taeniasis).
Diseases spread through air, water and food, vectors, contact and animal bites, so knowing the mode of spread guides prevention.
Immunity is innate or acquired; acquired immunity is active (long-lasting, body-made) or passive (short-lived, ready-made antibodies).
Vaccination builds active immunity and has eradicated smallpox and controlled polio, measles, tuberculosis and other diseases.
Lifestyle diseases (cancer, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension) and drug/alcohol abuse are controlled by healthy living, hygiene and awareness.

A protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen and helps destroy the pathogen.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Some Common Human Diseases (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write clear, well-organised answers. For long-answer questions give named examples of pathogens, vectors and diseases where relevant.

questions.question: Define health as given by the World Health Organisation, and distinguish between a sign and a symptom.
questions.answer:
The World Health Organisation defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

A SYMPTOM is a change that the patient feels and reports, such as pain, fever or weakness. A SIGN is a change that a doctor can observe or measure, such as a raised temperature, swelling or an abnormal blood count.

questions.question: Classify diseases into congenital and acquired, and further classify acquired diseases, giving one example of each type.
questions.answer:
Diseases are of two main kinds:

CONGENITAL diseases are present from birth and are usually due to genetic defects, e.g. haemophilia or Down's syndrome.

ACQUIRED diseases develop after birth. They are of two types:
- COMMUNICABLE (infectious), which spread from person to person, e.g. tuberculosis.
- NON-COMMUNICABLE, which do not spread, e.g. diabetes.
questions.explanation: Congenital vs acquired; acquired = communicable + non-communicable.

questions.question: Name the pathogen, mode of transmission and one prevention method for tuberculosis.
questions.answer: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It spreads through droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes (airborne). It is prevented by the BCG vaccine (and controlled by a full course of antibiotics under the DOTS programme).

questions.question: Why are antibiotics effective against bacterial diseases but not against viral diseases? How are viral diseases best prevented?
questions.answer:
Antibiotics act on structures and processes found in bacteria, such as their cell wall or protein-making machinery, so they kill or stop bacteria. Viruses have none of these; they are not truly cells and can multiply only inside the host's living cells, so antibiotics have no target to act on and do not work against them.

Viral diseases are best prevented by VACCINATION, which makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells against the virus, along with hygiene and avoiding contact with infected persons.
questions.explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial structures absent in viruses; prevent viruses by vaccines.

questions.question: Describe the life cycle of the malarial parasite, naming the pathogen and its vector, and state two ways of preventing malaria.
questions.answer:
Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium (species such as P. vivax and P. falciparum) and is transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito.

Life cycle: When an infected female Anopheles bites a person, it injects the parasite (sporozoites) with its saliva. These reach the LIVER, where they multiply. They then enter the RED BLOOD CELLS, multiply again, and destroy them. The bursting of red cells releases the parasites and toxins, which cause the typical symptoms of chill, high fever and sweating that recur in cycles. When another female Anopheles bites the infected person, it takes up the parasite, in which the parasite reproduces sexually, completing the cycle and making the mosquito infective again.

Prevention: (1) Destroy mosquito breeding places (remove stagnant water) and use nets, screens and repellents; (2) take antimalarial drugs and treat patients promptly to break the cycle.
questions.explanation: Plasmodium + female Anopheles; liver then RBC multiplication; two host cycle; prevention.

questions.question: Distinguish between active immunity and passive immunity, giving one example of each.
questions.answer:
ACTIVE immunity is produced by the body's own cells when it meets an antigen, through natural infection or vaccination. It develops slowly but lasts long because memory cells are formed. Example: immunity after the measles vaccine or after having measles.

PASSIVE immunity is provided by ready-made antibodies given from outside. It acts immediately but is short-lived because no memory cells are formed. Example: antibodies passed from mother to baby through the placenta or breast milk, or an anti-tetanus serum injection.
questions.explanation: Active = body-made, slow, long; passive = ready-made, immediate, short.

questions.question: How does vaccination protect a person from disease? Name any two diseases against which children are vaccinated in India.
questions.answer:
A vaccine contains weakened, killed or fragments of a pathogen (or its toxoid). When introduced into the body it stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and MEMORY cells against that pathogen, WITHOUT causing the disease. If the real pathogen later attacks, the memory cells recognise it and the body destroys it quickly, so the person does not fall ill. This is active immunity.

In India children are vaccinated against tuberculosis (BCG), diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus (DPT), polio (OPV), measles and hepatitis B (any two).
questions.explanation: Vaccine builds antibodies + memory cells; names two vaccine-preventable diseases.

questions.question: What is diabetes mellitus? State its main cause and two ways of controlling it.
questions.answer:
Diabetes mellitus is a non-communicable disease in which the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood rises above normal.

Cause: It results when the pancreas fails to produce enough of the hormone INSULIN, or the body cannot use insulin properly, so glucose is not taken up by cells and accumulates in the blood.

Control: (1) a controlled diet and regular exercise with weight control; (2) medicines or insulin injections as advised by a doctor.
questions.explanation: Raised blood sugar from insulin failure; diet/exercise and medicine/insulin.

questions.question: What is drug abuse? Explain the terms addiction, tolerance and withdrawal, and suggest two ways to prevent drug abuse among youth.
questions.answer:
DRUG ABUSE is the use of a drug for a purpose other than medical, in a way and amount that harms the body and mind.

ADDICTION (dependence) is a state in which a person cannot do without the drug and craves it constantly.

TOLERANCE is the condition in which repeated use makes the body need larger and larger doses to get the same effect.

WITHDRAWAL refers to the unpleasant physical and mental symptoms (such as anxiety, sweating, pain and shaking) that appear when an addicted person stops the drug.

Prevention: (1) create awareness about the harmful effects and encourage youth to say NO to peer pressure; (2) provide counselling, healthy recreation, and help through de-addiction centres with support from family and friends.
questions.explanation: Definitions of abuse, addiction, tolerance, withdrawal; two prevention measures.

questions.question: List any four measures of personal and community hygiene that help prevent the spread of diseases.
questions.answer:
Personal hygiene: (1) washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet; (2) bathing regularly and keeping nails, teeth and clothes clean.

Community hygiene: (3) providing safe drinking water and proper disposal of sewage and garbage; (4) controlling insects (mosquitoes, houseflies) and rodents and keeping surroundings clean. (Safe food handling and vaccination also help.)
questions.explanation: Two personal + two community hygiene measures.

questions.question: Diseases present from birth are called ____ diseases.
Infectious diseases that spread from person to person are also called ____ diseases.
Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio ____.
AIDS is caused by the virus known as ____.
Rabies is transmitted by the ____ of an infected animal.
____ are effective against bacteria but not against viruses.
Malaria is caused by the protozoan ____.
In the human body, the malarial parasite multiplies in the liver and in the ____ blood cells.
questions.explanation: RBCs are destroyed by the parasite.

questions.question: Filariasis is transmitted by the ____ mosquito.
A foreign substance that triggers an immune response is called an ____.
Immunity produced by giving ready-made antibodies is called ____ immunity.
A vaccine builds ____ immunity in the body.
Diabetes mellitus results from a lack or poor action of the hormone ____.
Persistently high blood pressure is called ____.
The unpleasant symptoms felt when an addict stops taking a drug are called ____ symptoms.
Define disease and give the difference between a sign and a symptom.
questions.answer: A DISEASE is any disturbance in the normal structure or functioning of the body (or a part of it) that produces recognisable signs and symptoms. A SYMPTOM is a change the patient feels and reports (e.g. pain, fever); a SIGN is a change the doctor can observe or measure (e.g. raised temperature, swelling).

questions.question: Distinguish between communicable and non-communicable diseases with one example each.
questions.answer: COMMUNICABLE (infectious) diseases are caused by pathogens and spread from an infected person to a healthy person, e.g. tuberculosis. NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases do not spread from person to person and arise from lifestyle, deficiency or malfunction of organs, e.g. diabetes.

questions.question: Give two examples each of congenital and acquired diseases.
questions.answer: Congenital diseases (present from birth): haemophilia and Down's syndrome (also colour blindness, sickle-cell anaemia). Acquired diseases (develop after birth): tuberculosis and diabetes (also cholera, cancer).

questions.question: Name the pathogen and mode of spread of cholera, and one way to prevent it.
questions.answer: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. It spreads through contaminated water and food. It is prevented by using safe (boiled/clean) drinking water and proper sanitation; oral rehydration therapy is used for treatment.

questions.question: Describe how AIDS spreads and two ways it does NOT spread.
questions.answer: AIDS is caused by HIV. It spreads through: unprotected sexual contact with an infected person; transfusion of infected blood; sharing of infected needles/syringes; and from an infected mother to her child. It does NOT spread by casual contact such as shaking hands, hugging, sharing food or utensils, or by mosquito bites.

questions.question: State the cause, symptoms and prevention of tetanus.
questions.answer: Tetanus (lockjaw) is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, whose spores enter through deep wounds. Its toxin causes painful muscle spasms and stiffness, especially locking of the jaw. It is prevented by the DPT vaccine in childhood and tetanus toxoid injections after injuries.

questions.question: Name any four viral diseases of humans.
questions.answer: Four viral diseases: common cold, influenza, measles and polio (others include hepatitis, rabies, dengue, AIDS and COVID-19).

questions.question: What is hepatitis? How do hepatitis A and hepatitis B differ in their spread?
questions.answer: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis viruses; a common sign is jaundice. Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water, while hepatitis B spreads through infected blood, body fluids and unsafe injections. Vaccines exist for both A and B.
questions.explanation: Liver inflammation; A food/water, B blood/fluids.

questions.question: Why do doctors advise against taking antibiotics for a common cold?
questions.answer: The common cold is caused by a virus (rhinovirus). Antibiotics act on structures and processes found only in bacteria, which viruses do not have, so antibiotics cannot kill viruses or cure the cold. Misusing antibiotics wastes them and can make bacteria resistant. Rest, fluids and time allow recovery.
questions.explanation: Cold is viral; antibiotics target bacteria only.

questions.question: Give two differences between bacterial and viral diseases.
questions.answer: 1) Cause: bacterial diseases are caused by bacteria (living cells that can multiply on their own), while viral diseases are caused by viruses (that multiply only inside host cells). 2) Treatment: bacterial diseases can be treated with antibiotics, but viral diseases cannot; they are prevented mainly by vaccines. (Examples: TB is bacterial; measles is viral.)

questions.question: Name the pathogen and vector of malaria and describe its symptoms.
questions.answer: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. As the parasite multiplies in and bursts out of red blood cells it releases toxins, causing recurring cycles of shivering/chill, high fever and then sweating, along with headache and weakness.

questions.question: What is ringworm and how does it spread?
questions.answer: Ringworm is a fungal disease of the skin, scalp or nails that produces dry, scaly, itchy ring-shaped patches. It is caused by fungi (such as Microsporum and Trichophyton) and spreads by contact with infected persons, animals or shared objects like combs and towels; heat and moisture favour it.
questions.explanation: Fungal skin disease; spreads by contact.

questions.question: Name three helminthic (worm) diseases and the worm causing each.
questions.answer: 1) Ascariasis - caused by the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. 2) Filariasis (elephantiasis) - caused by the filarial worm Wuchereria (spread by the Culex mosquito). 3) Taeniasis - caused by the tapeworm Taenia (from undercooked pork or beef).

questions.question: How can mosquito-borne diseases be prevented?
questions.answer: By destroying mosquito breeding places (removing stagnant water, covering water tanks), spraying insecticides, using mosquito nets, screens and repellents, wearing full-covering clothes, and treating patients promptly to break the transmission cycle.

questions.question: Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity.
questions.answer: INNATE (natural, non-specific) immunity is present from birth and acts against any invader; its defences include the skin, mucous membranes, secretions and phagocytic white blood cells. ACQUIRED (specific) immunity develops during life after exposure to a particular pathogen; it is specific and has MEMORY, so the body responds faster on a second exposure.
questions.explanation: Innate = inborn, non-specific; acquired = specific, memory.

questions.question: What are antigens and antibodies? State their relationship.
questions.answer: An ANTIGEN is any foreign substance (usually a protein on a pathogen) that triggers an immune response. An ANTIBODY is a protein made by the body's lymphocytes in response to an antigen. Each antibody binds specifically to its antigen and neutralises or helps destroy the pathogen. Thus antigens stimulate the production of matching antibodies.
questions.explanation: Antigen triggers; antibody binds and destroys.

questions.question: Briefly outline the immune response when a pathogen enters the body.
questions.answer: When a pathogen enters, phagocytic cells engulf some of it and display its antigens. Helper T-lymphocytes recognise these antigens and activate B-lymphocytes, which multiply and secrete ANTIBODIES that neutralise the pathogen, while other cells destroy infected cells. Some cells become MEMORY cells that remember the antigen, so a later attack by the same pathogen is met faster and more strongly.

questions.question: What is a vaccine? Explain how vaccination prevents disease.
questions.answer: A VACCINE is a preparation of weakened, killed or fragments of a pathogen (or its toxoid). On being introduced into the body it stimulates the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells WITHOUT causing the disease. If the real pathogen attacks later, the memory cells respond quickly and the body destroys it before illness develops. This is active immunity.

questions.question: Name four diseases against which children are immunised under India's programme, with the vaccine used.
questions.answer: Tuberculosis (BCG vaccine); diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus (DPT vaccine); poliomyelitis (oral polio vaccine, OPV); measles (measles/MMR vaccine); hepatitis B (hepatitis B vaccine). Any four of these are acceptable.
questions.explanation: BCG, DPT, OPV, measles/MMR, hepatitis B.

questions.question: What is cancer? State two causes and one method of treatment.
questions.answer: Cancer is the uncontrolled, abnormal multiplication of body cells that have lost the normal checks on division; the mass formed is a tumour, and a malignant tumour can spread to other organs (metastasis). Causes include tobacco and alcohol, radiation, cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens), some viruses and heredity. It is treated by surgery, radiation therapy or chemotherapy, especially if detected early.

questions.question: Why is hypertension called a silent killer? How can it be controlled?
questions.answer: Hypertension (high blood pressure) usually shows no clear symptoms, yet it silently strains the heart, blood vessels, kidneys and brain and can lead to heart attack or stroke - hence 'silent killer'. It is controlled by a low-salt and low-fat diet, regular exercise, maintaining normal weight, avoiding smoking and alcohol, reducing stress, and taking medicines as prescribed.
questions.explanation: No symptoms but damaging; diet/exercise/medicine control.

questions.question: Suggest four measures to prevent and control the spread of infectious diseases in a community.
questions.answer: 1) Provide safe drinking water and proper disposal of sewage and garbage; 2) maintain personal hygiene - wash hands, keep the body and food clean; 3) control disease-carrying insects and rodents (remove stagnant water, use nets); 4) vaccinate children and adults, and isolate infected patients with sterilisation of instruments and safe blood transfusion.

questions.question: Explain the classification of human diseases with a suitable scheme and examples.
questions.answer:
Human diseases can be classified as follows.

1) CONGENITAL diseases are present from birth, usually due to genetic defects or problems during development, e.g. haemophilia, colour blindness, sickle-cell anaemia and Down's syndrome. They are often inherited and permanent.

2) ACQUIRED diseases develop after birth during a person's life. They are of two kinds:

   a) COMMUNICABLE (infectious) diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi, worms) and spread from an infected person to a healthy one - e.g. tuberculosis, cholera, malaria, influenza and AIDS.

   b) NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases do not spread from person to person. They arise from lifestyle, deficiency, degeneration or malfunction of organs - e.g. cancer, diabetes, hypertension and heart disease.

Thus the main scheme is: Diseases -> Congenital / Acquired; and Acquired -> Communicable / Non-communicable.
questions.explanation: Congenital vs acquired; acquired into communicable/non-communicable with examples.

questions.question: Describe any four bacterial diseases, stating the pathogen, mode of spread, symptoms and prevention of each.
questions.answer:
1) TUBERCULOSIS - pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis; spreads by droplets (air); symptoms: persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss; prevented by BCG vaccine and treated under DOTS.

2) CHOLERA - pathogen Vibrio cholerae; spreads by contaminated water/food; symptoms: severe watery diarrhoea, vomiting, dehydration; prevented by safe water and sanitation, treated with oral rehydration.

3) TYPHOID - pathogen Salmonella typhi; spreads by contaminated food/water; symptoms: sustained high fever, headache, weakness, abdominal pain; prevented by hygiene and vaccination.

4) TETANUS - pathogen Clostridium tetani entering through deep wounds; symptoms: painful muscle spasms and jaw stiffness (lockjaw); prevented by DPT vaccine and tetanus toxoid. (Pneumonia and diphtheria are other examples.)
questions.explanation: Four bacterial diseases with pathogen, spread, symptoms, prevention.

questions.question: Compare bacterial and viral diseases and analyse why their treatment differs.
questions.answer:
BACTERIAL diseases are caused by bacteria, which are complete living cells with their own cell wall, membrane and machinery to make proteins and reproduce on their own (e.g. TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus). VIRAL diseases are caused by viruses, which are not truly cells; they lack their own machinery and can multiply only inside a host's living cells (e.g. common cold, influenza, measles, AIDS).

Treatment differs because ANTIBIOTICS act on structures and processes unique to bacteria, such as the bacterial cell wall or protein-making system. They kill bacteria or stop their growth, so bacterial diseases are curable with antibiotics. Viruses have none of these bacterial targets and hide inside the body's own cells, so antibiotics cannot act on them. Therefore viral diseases are not cured by antibiotics; they are prevented mainly by VACCINES that build immunity, and managed with rest, fluids and, in some cases, antiviral drugs. Misuse of antibiotics for viral illness is useless and promotes antibiotic resistance.
questions.explanation: Cell vs non-cell; antibiotic target present in bacteria, absent in viruses.

questions.question: Explain the life cycle of the malarial parasite in the human host and the mosquito, and how malaria is controlled.
questions.answer:
Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito, which needs two hosts to complete its life cycle.

In the HUMAN host: When an infected female Anopheles bites a person, it injects the parasite (sporozoites) with its saliva. These travel to the LIVER, where they multiply. They then leave the liver and enter the RED BLOOD CELLS, where they multiply again and finally burst the cells. The bursting releases parasites and toxins, causing the typical recurring chill, high fever and sweating.

In the MOSQUITO host: When another female Anopheles bites the infected person, it sucks up the parasites in the blood. Inside the mosquito the parasite reproduces SEXUALLY, forming new infective stages that move to the mosquito's salivary glands, making it able to infect the next person.

Control: destroy mosquito breeding places (remove stagnant water), spray insecticides, use nets and repellents, and treat patients promptly with antimalarial drugs to break the cycle.
questions.explanation: Two-host cycle: human liver+RBC, mosquito sexual stage; control measures.

questions.question: Explain the different types of immunity with examples.
questions.answer:
IMMUNITY is the body's ability to resist and fight pathogens. It is of two broad types.

1) INNATE (natural, non-specific) immunity is present from birth and acts against any invader. Its defences are the skin and mucous membranes (physical barriers), acids and enzymes in secretions (chemical barriers), and phagocytic white blood cells, inflammation and fever.

2) ACQUIRED (specific) immunity develops after exposure to a particular pathogen and has MEMORY. It is of two kinds:
   - ACTIVE immunity is made by the body's own cells after a natural infection or vaccination. It develops slowly but lasts long because memory cells are formed (e.g. immunity after measles or its vaccine).
   - PASSIVE immunity is provided by ready-made antibodies received from outside. It acts at once but is short-lived (e.g. antibodies passed from mother to baby, or an anti-tetanus serum injection).

Thus immunity may be inborn (innate) or developed (acquired), and acquired immunity may be active or passive.
questions.explanation: Innate vs acquired; acquired into active and passive with examples.

questions.question: What is immunisation? Explain how vaccines work and describe India's efforts to control diseases through immunisation.
questions.answer:
IMMUNISATION (vaccination) is the deliberate introduction of a vaccine into the body to build protective immunity against a disease. A VACCINE contains weakened, killed or fragments of a pathogen, or its inactivated toxin (toxoid).

How it works: The vaccine's antigens stimulate the immune system to produce ANTIBODIES and MEMORY cells without causing the disease. If the real pathogen enters later, the memory cells recognise it and the body destroys it quickly, so the person does not fall ill. This is active immunity, and it can be boosted by repeat doses.

India's efforts: The Universal Immunisation Programme protects children against tuberculosis (BCG), diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus (DPT), polio (OPV), measles and hepatitis B. The Pulse Polio programme gave oral polio drops to all young children on fixed days and has made India polio-free. Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine and worldwide immunisation earlier eradicated smallpox completely. When enough people are immunised, herd immunity protects even the unvaccinated.
questions.explanation: Immunisation; vaccine builds antibodies+memory; UIP, Pulse Polio, smallpox.

questions.question: Describe any three non-communicable (lifestyle) diseases, giving their causes, symptoms and control.
questions.answer:
1) CANCER is uncontrolled, abnormal multiplication of body cells forming tumours that may spread (metastasis). Causes: tobacco, alcohol, radiation, carcinogenic chemicals, some viruses and heredity. Symptoms depend on the site (e.g. lump, unusual bleeding, weight loss). Control: avoid tobacco and known carcinogens; early detection and treatment by surgery, radiation or chemotherapy.

2) DIABETES MELLITUS results when the pancreas makes too little insulin or the body cannot use it, so blood sugar rises. Symptoms: frequent urination, excessive thirst and hunger, weakness. Control: balanced diet, exercise, weight control, medicines or insulin.

3) HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure) is persistently raised blood pressure, often with no symptoms, that strains the heart, kidneys and brain. Control: low-salt diet, exercise, weight control, no smoking/alcohol, and medicines. (Cardiovascular/heart disease is another example.)
questions.explanation: Cancer, diabetes, hypertension: causes, symptoms, control.

questions.question: Discuss drug and alcohol abuse, its effects on health and society, and measures to prevent it.
questions.answer:
A DRUG is a chemical that changes body function; some are medicines, but many are misused. DRUG ABUSE is using a drug for a non-medical purpose in a harmful way. Commonly abused substances include opioids (opium, heroin), cannabinoids (ganja, charas), cocaine, and tobacco and alcohol.

Repeated use leads to ADDICTION (the person cannot do without it), TOLERANCE (larger doses are needed for the same effect) and WITHDRAWAL symptoms on stopping. Effects on health: damage to the liver (alcohol causes cirrhosis), brain, heart, lungs and nervous system; tobacco causes cancer of the lung and mouth; impaired judgement leads to accidents. Effects on society: broken studies and work, financial ruin, crime, and destroyed family and social relationships; drunk driving causes road accidents.

Prevention: create awareness of the harmful effects; help youth resist peer pressure and say NO; encourage healthy recreation, sports and hobbies; provide counselling and support from parents, teachers and friends; and use de-addiction and rehabilitation centres for treatment.
questions.explanation: Abuse, addiction/tolerance/withdrawal; health and social harm; prevention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A doctor examines a school where several children have symptoms. Some children have persistent cough spread by droplets in a crowded classroom; another child has a genetic bleeding disorder present since birth; a teacher has high blood sugar that does not spread to others.
(a) Classify the genetic bleeding disorder as congenital or acquired.
(b) Is the coughing illness communicable or non-communicable? Give a reason.
(c) Classify the teacher's high-blood-sugar condition.
(d) Distinguish between a sign and a symptom.
questions.answer:
(a) The genetic bleeding disorder (haemophilia) is CONGENITAL - present from birth due to a genetic defect.
(b) The coughing illness is COMMUNICABLE (infectious), because it spreads from one child to others through droplets in the air.
(c) The teacher's condition (diabetes) is a NON-COMMUNICABLE disease; it does not spread from person to person.
(d) A SIGN is a change a doctor can observe or measure (e.g. fever, swelling); a SYMPTOM is a change the patient feels and reports (e.g. pain, tiredness).
questions.explanation: Applies the congenital/acquired and communicable/non-communicable classification.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
During the rainy season a town reports many cases of watery diarrhoea and vomiting leading to dehydration. Tests show the bacterium Vibrio cholerae in drinking water drawn from a contaminated well.
(a) Name the disease and its pathogen.
(b) How is the disease spreading in the town?
(c) Give the immediate treatment for a dehydrated patient.
(d) Suggest two measures to prevent further spread.
questions.answer:
(a) The disease is CHOLERA, caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.
(b) It is spreading through contaminated drinking water (and food) from the polluted well - a water-borne disease.
(c) Immediate treatment is ORAL REHYDRATION THERAPY (ORS solution) to replace lost water and salts, along with medical care.
(d) Prevention: (i) provide safe, boiled or chlorinated drinking water and stop using the contaminated well; (ii) ensure proper sanitation and disposal of waste, and maintain personal and food hygiene.
questions.explanation: Cholera: pathogen, water-borne spread, ORS, prevention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A health worker counsels a community about HIV/AIDS. Some people fear that they can catch AIDS by sitting next to, sharing food with, or shaking hands with an infected person.
(a) Name the virus that causes AIDS and the cells it destroys.
(b) State two real ways in which HIV spreads.
(c) Are the community's fears about casual contact correct? Explain.
(d) Suggest one way to prevent the spread of AIDS.
questions.answer:
(a) AIDS is caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), which destroys the helper T-lymphocytes of the immune system.
(b) HIV spreads through: transfusion of infected blood or sharing of infected needles; unprotected sexual contact; and from an infected mother to her child (any two).
(c) No, the fears are NOT correct. HIV does not spread by casual contact such as shaking hands, sitting together or sharing food, because the virus is not transmitted through such everyday contact.
(d) Prevention: use only tested/safe blood and sterile needles, practise safe behaviour, and spread awareness (any one).
questions.explanation: Analyses HIV transmission and dispels casual-contact myths.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A patient with a viral fever is given antibiotics by a chemist without a prescription, but does not improve. A doctor later explains that antibiotics cannot cure viral diseases.
(a) Why do antibiotics not work against viruses?
(b) Against which type of pathogen do antibiotics work?
(c) How are viral diseases best prevented?
(d) State one harm of misusing antibiotics.
questions.answer:
(a) Antibiotics act on structures and processes found only in bacteria (such as the cell wall or protein-making machinery). Viruses lack these and multiply inside the body's own cells, so antibiotics have no target to act on.
(b) Antibiotics work against BACTERIA.
(c) Viral diseases are best prevented by VACCINATION, along with hygiene and avoiding contact with infected persons.
(d) Misuse of antibiotics wastes them and promotes ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE, so they may fail to work when really needed (also side effects).
questions.explanation: Analyses why antibiotics fail against viruses; prevention and resistance.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a village near stagnant pools, many people suffer from recurring bouts of chill, high fever and sweating. A blood test shows the parasite Plasmodium in their red blood cells.
(a) Name the disease and the mosquito that spreads it.
(b) Why do the fever cycles occur?
(c) Where in the human body does the parasite first multiply?
(d) Suggest two ways to control the disease in the village.
questions.answer:
(a) The disease is MALARIA, spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.
(b) The fever cycles occur when the parasite multiplies in and bursts out of the RED BLOOD CELLS, releasing parasites and toxins into the blood.
(c) In the human body the parasite first multiplies in the LIVER, then enters the red blood cells.
(d) Control: (i) destroy mosquito breeding places by removing/draining stagnant water and spraying insecticide; (ii) use mosquito nets and repellents and treat patients promptly with antimalarial drugs.
questions.explanation: Malaria life cycle and vector control applied to a village.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A child has itchy, dry, ring-shaped patches on the scalp and skin. The doctor says it is caused by a fungus and can pass to others who share the child's comb and towel.
(a) Name the disease.
(b) What kind of organism causes it?
(c) How does it spread?
(d) Suggest two ways to prevent its spread.
questions.answer:
(a) The disease is RINGWORM.
(b) It is caused by a FUNGUS (such as Microsporum or Trichophyton).
(c) It spreads by contact - directly with an infected person or animal, or indirectly through shared objects such as combs, towels and clothes; heat and moisture help it grow.
(d) Prevention: (i) do not share combs, towels, clothes or other personal items; (ii) keep the skin clean and dry, and treat the infection with antifungal medicine.
questions.explanation: Applies knowledge of fungal ringworm spread and prevention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A newborn baby receives protective antibodies through its mother's breast milk. Months later the same baby is given a measles vaccine so that its own body makes antibodies against measles.
(a) Name the type of immunity the baby gets from breast milk.
(b) Name the type of immunity produced by the measles vaccine.
(c) Which of these two is longer-lasting and why?
(d) What is the general name for a foreign substance that triggers antibody production?
questions.answer:
(a) From breast milk the baby gets PASSIVE immunity (ready-made antibodies from the mother).
(b) The measles vaccine produces ACTIVE immunity (the baby's own body makes antibodies).
(c) ACTIVE immunity is longer-lasting, because the body forms MEMORY cells that continue to protect for a long time; passive immunity is short-lived as no memory cells are made.
(d) A foreign substance that triggers antibody production is called an ANTIGEN.
questions.explanation: Distinguishes passive vs active immunity with duration and antigen.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Health workers visit homes on a fixed Sunday to give polio drops to every child under five years, as part of a national campaign. Posters explain that this will keep the country free of polio.
(a) Name the programme and the vaccine used.
(b) What type of immunity does the vaccine produce?
(c) How does the vaccine protect the child?
(d) What is meant by herd immunity?
questions.answer:
(a) The programme is the PULSE POLIO programme, and the vaccine used is the ORAL POLIO VACCINE (OPV).
(b) It produces ACTIVE immunity.
(c) The vaccine contains weakened poliovirus that makes the child's body produce antibodies and memory cells without causing polio; if the real virus enters later, the body destroys it quickly.
(d) HERD IMMUNITY means that when a large majority of a community is immunised, the disease cannot spread easily, so even the few unvaccinated people are protected.
questions.explanation: Applies vaccination and immunisation-programme ideas to Pulse Polio.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A middle-aged man with an office job eats a lot of fatty and sugary food, does no exercise, is overweight and smokes. A check-up shows raised blood sugar and high blood pressure.
(a) Name the two diseases indicated by his reports.
(b) Which hormone is linked to the raised blood sugar?
(c) Why are these called lifestyle diseases?
(d) Suggest two changes he should make to improve his health.
questions.answer:
(a) The two diseases are DIABETES MELLITUS (raised blood sugar) and HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure).
(b) The hormone linked to blood sugar is INSULIN (made by the pancreas).
(c) They are called lifestyle diseases because they result largely from the way of living - poor diet, lack of exercise, obesity, stress and smoking - rather than from an infecting pathogen.
(d) He should: (i) eat a balanced, low-fat, low-sugar and low-salt diet and lose weight through regular exercise; (ii) stop smoking and reduce stress, and follow the doctor's advice/medicines.
questions.explanation: Analyses lifestyle risk factors for diabetes and hypertension.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A teenager begins using a drug offered by friends. Over time he needs larger amounts to feel the same effect, feels sick and anxious when he stops, and cannot do without it. His studies and family life suffer.
(a) What is this harmful use of the drug called?
(b) Name the condition in which he needs larger doses for the same effect.
(c) Name the symptoms he feels when he stops the drug.
(d) Suggest two ways to help him recover.
questions.answer:
(a) This harmful, non-medical use of the drug is called DRUG ABUSE, and his dependence on it is ADDICTION.
(b) Needing larger doses for the same effect is called TOLERANCE.
(c) The unpleasant symptoms felt on stopping are called WITHDRAWAL symptoms.
(d) Help: (i) counselling and treatment at a de-addiction/rehabilitation centre; (ii) support and encouragement from family, friends and teachers, with healthy recreation and avoiding the company that offers drugs.
questions.explanation: Applies concepts of abuse, tolerance, withdrawal and rehabilitation.
